articles.title: Edmonton Elks beat Montreal 37-30 to win the 113th Grey Cup at McMahon Stadium
articles.dek: Calgary's sixth Grey Cup ended with Edmonton's first championship since 2015, and Tourism Calgary estimates the week brought about $50 million in economic activity.
body: The Edmonton Elks won the 113th Grey Cup on Sunday, Nov. 15, defeating the Montreal Alouettes 37-30 at McMahon Stadium in Calgary [1][2]. It is the club's 15th Grey Cup since it was founded in 1949 and its first since 2015, when the team, then called the Eskimos, beat Ottawa 26-20 [1].

Quarterback Cody Fajardo was named the game's most valuable player, his second Grey Cup MVP award in four years [2]. He threw for 199 yards with two touchdown passes and one interception, and ran for 45 yards and two more touchdowns [2]. Montreal had released Fajardo a year after he led the Alouettes to the 2023 championship [1]. Rookie receiver Joshua Cephus caught two touchdown passes, including the go-ahead score in the third quarter, and running back Justin Rankin ran for 85 yards [2].

The game swung back and forth. Edmonton led 21-17 at halftime and 31-24 going into the fourth quarter [3]. Montreal quarterback Davis Alexander, the league's most outstanding player this season, completed 21 of 36 passes for 226 yards and a touchdown but hurt his shoulder late in the third quarter [2]. Alouettes receiver Tyson Philpot was named the game's most valuable Canadian, the first player from the losing side to win the award since 2017 [2]. Montreal kicked its final field goal with five seconds left [2].

Both teams had finished first in their divisions. Edmonton went 13-5 and beat the B.C. Lions 28-16 in the West final, while Montreal went 14-4 and beat the Winnipeg Blue Bombers 33-23 in the East final [1]. The Elks' turnaround began in 2024, when the team was sold to the late Larry Thompson and his wife, Deb Thompson [1][2].

Pre-game entertainment included the James Barker Band and Blue Rodeo, with Sarah McLachlan singing the anthem, and Riley Green performed at halftime [3]. The temperature at kickoff was about 14 degrees [3]. It was Calgary's sixth time hosting the Grey Cup, after 2019, and the Calgary Journal noted it could be the last one played at McMahon Stadium [3].

Tourism Calgary estimates the Grey Cup festivities brought about $50 million in economic activity to the city [4]. Steve Sommerfeld chaired the Calgary Grey Cup Committee, which opened the festival week on Thursday, Nov. 12 [4]. Elks head coach Mark Kilam summed up his team after the win: "We're not a sexy team." [2]

Cody Fajardo named Grey Cup MVP; Tyson Philpot top Canadian

articles.title: Water use rose to 490 million litres on Grey Cup Sunday but stayed under the limit
articles.dek: Calgary has now stayed under its 500-million-litre daily target for 12 straight days as Bearspaw South feeder main tie-in work passes the halfway mark.
body: Calgarians used 490 million litres of water on Sunday, Nov. 15, the day of the Grey Cup, city officials said Monday [1][2][3]. That was up from 477 million litres on Saturday but still under the 500-million-litre daily target set while the Bearspaw South feeder main is out of service [2]. CTV News reported the Sunday figure as a 16-million-litre rise over the day before, which does not match the Saturday figure the city gave the Calgary Herald [3][2].

The city has stayed in the green zone every day for 12 days, since temporary Stage 4 water restrictions took effect on Nov. 4 [2]. Mayor Jeromy Farkas said use stayed below typical levels even with about 35,000 visitors in town for the game [1]. "We're bringing the green zone to the end zone," Farkas said [2].

Farkas said the project is nearly halfway complete [2]. The Canadian Press described the city as about halfway through roughly three weeks of restrictions [1]. The Stage 4 rules stay in place until the Bearspaw South feeder main is back in service; that line carries about 60 per cent of Calgary's treated water [2]. No end date has been announced [2].

Crews are joining the new steel pipe to the existing feeder main at three sites: the Shaganappi Pump Station near Edworthy Park, where pipe sections were placed and welded over the weekend; 33 Avenue and 89 Street N.W., where excavation is finished and the last pipe pieces are going in; and 83 Street N.W., where digging is under way [2].

Separate work on the 1,500-millimetre feeder main between the Shaganappi and Memorial pump stations has been postponed at one of six planned sites, which lies under a park, until next year because of a leaky valve; that work does not need restrictions [2]. A repair to a leak on the Edgemont feeder main is also under way, and residents of Edgemont, the Hamptons, Citadel, Hawkwood and Arbour Lake may see temporary low water pressure, though the water remains safe to drink [2].
The restrictions are meant to keep the water treatment plant from being strained and to keep enough water on hand for firefighting [1].
key_facts: Sunday, Nov. 15: 490 million litres; Saturday: 477 million litres
12 straight days under the target since Stage 4 began Nov. 4

articles.title: Alberta tables bill to put new electoral map into law, including hybrid Calgary divisions
articles.dek: The legislation would raise the number of seats from 87 to 91 before the October 2027 election; the Opposition NDP says it will challenge the map in court.
body: The Alberta government on Monday, Nov. 16, tabled legislation to put new electoral division boundaries into law ahead of the next provincial general election, scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027 [1][2]. The bill's number and name were not given in the reports.

The new map would raise the number of seats in the legislature from 87 to 91, as recommended in an advisory panel report published earlier in November [1]. It includes hybrid electoral divisions that combine some urban voters in Calgary and Lethbridge with surrounding rural areas [1]. In Lethbridge, the city's two current urban divisions would become four: one entirely urban and three hybrids, some of them reaching the U.S. border [1]. The reports did not say how many Calgary divisions would change.

The map follows a change of course earlier this year. Premier Danielle Smith's government voted down the proposals of the public electoral boundaries commission, then appointed a committee to oversee a new advisory panel with a chair appointed by the governing United Conservative Party [1]. UCP members were unanimous in a symbolic vote earlier this month endorsing the changes [1].

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said the new divisions dilute urban votes to benefit the UCP and called the plan "very likely unconstitutional" [1]. He said the party will challenge the law in court but must wait until it receives royal assent before filing [1].

The government denies trying to tilt the 2027 election. It says the map improves effective representation and points out that hybrid divisions already exist elsewhere in Alberta [1]. Justice Minister Mickey Amery described hybrid divisions as the way of the future and dismissed the possible court challenge as sour grapes [1].
The bill must pass the legislature and receive royal assent before it takes effect [1][2].
key_facts: Some Calgary voters would be placed in hybrid urban-rural divisions
NDP plans a court challenge after royal assent

articles.title: Thirty-five people killed in crashes on Calgary roads so far in 2026, police say
articles.dek: Police count 29 fatal collisions this year, a pace that would top 2025, which was already the deadliest year in a decade by mid-November.
body: Calgary police say 29 fatal collisions on city roads so far in 2026 have killed 35 people, CTV News reported on Monday, Nov. 16 [1]. The report says this year's death toll is on pace to surpass 2025 [1]. Police did not give a full-year 2025 figure in the material available.

Last year was already a high-water mark. In a joint release on Nov. 14, 2025, the Calgary Police Service and the City of Calgary said there had been 31 fatal collisions with 31 deaths to that point in 2025, a 10-year high [2]. More than 2,500 collisions that year had injured drivers, passengers, pedestrians, cyclists or motorcyclists [2].

The 2025 release broke down the fatal crashes to that date. Speed was a factor in 12 of the 31, three were hit-and-runs, and at least four involved drugs or alcohol, with some toxicology results still pending [2]. Twenty, or about 65 per cent, involved a pedestrian, motorcyclist or cyclist [2].
Over the past decade, the number of fatal collisions in Calgary has ranged from 11 in 2017 to 29 in 2024, according to the city's figures [2]. Injury collisions peaked at 2,903 in 2024 [2].

The city's Safer Mobility Plan follows a Vision Zero approach that aims to eliminate traffic deaths and major injuries [2]. Pat Grisak, the city's senior leader of traffic management, said at the time: "One death on our roads is too many." [2] The World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims is marked on the third Sunday of November each year, and the 2025 release was issued ahead of that day [2].
A photo with the CTV report shows fire crews at a deadly three-vehicle crash on Stoney Trail in southwest Calgary on Aug. 2, 2026 [1].
key_facts: By mid-November 2025: 31 fatal collisions, a 10-year high
About 65% of 2025's fatal crashes to that date involved pedestrians, cyclists or motorcyclists

articles.title: Trial hears of handgun drawn in Martindale temple parking lot during 2024 confrontation
articles.dek: Two men face threat and firearms charges; a witness told a Calgary court one of them pulled a gun from his waistband during an argument.
body: The Calgary Court of Justice is hearing the trial of two men accused of threatening a man outside a Sikh temple in the northeast community of Martindale in September 2024, the Calgary Herald reported on Monday, Nov. 16 [1]. None of the allegations has been proven in court.

Gursewak Singh, 34, and Sukhpreet Singh, 24, each face a charge of uttering threats dated Sept. 24, 2024, along with four firearms-related charges [1]. Gursewak Singh faces five further counts, including pointing a firearm, possessing a stolen firearm and possessing opium [1]. The case is being heard by Justice Judith Shriar [1].

The witness, whose home had been shot at days earlier, testified that he had just left a meeting at the Dashmesh Cultural Centre when he was approached in the parking lot [1]. He said he and Gursewak Singh had a loud argument, during which he asked whether Gursewak Singh was behind the shooting at his home and a threatening phone call [1]. The witness told the court Gursewak Singh pulled a gun from his waistband and waved it toward the group [1]. Cellphone videos shown in court, recorded in Punjabi, show a silver handgun [1].

Asked by Crown prosecutor Matt Dalidowicz how he felt, the witness said anybody would have been scared [1]. In the Crown's opening, the court heard that police found a loaded .357 revolver in Gursewak Singh's waistband and a loaded 9mm pistol in an inside jacket pocket worn by Sukhpreet Singh [1]. The witness said the gun was no longer in Gursewak Singh's hand when police arrived [1].

Gursewak Singh is also scheduled to stand trial next week on allegations related to the Sept. 19, 2024 shooting at the witness's home and an extortion allegation [1]. The accused have not been convicted of any offence.
key_facts: Two men face threat and firearms charges from Sept. 24, 2024
Confrontation alleged in the parking lot of a Martindale Sikh temple
A second trial on a related home shooting and extortion is set for next week
